units.text: INT. FAN - CONTINUOUS

No, I am talking very seriously. You mustn’t laugh, I am quite serious. I don’t like compliments, and I don’t see why a man should think he is pleasing a woman enormously when he says to her a whole heap of things that he doesn’t mean.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Ah, but I did mean them.
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: Takes tea which she offers him .
Gravely .

I hope not. I should be sorry to have to quarrel with you, Lord Darlington. I like you very much, you know that. But I shouldn’t like you at all if I thought you were what most other men are. Believe me, you are better than most other men, and I sometimes think you pretend to be worse.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: We all have our little vanities, Lady Windermere.
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: Why do you make that your special one?
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Still seated at table L.
Still seated L.C.

Oh, nowadays so many conceited people go about Society pretending to be good, that I think it shows rather a sweet and modest disposition to pretend to be bad. Besides, there is this to be said. If you pretend to be good, the world takes you very seriously. If you pretend to be bad, it doesn’t. Such is the astounding stupidity of optimism.
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: Don’t you want the world to take you seriously then, Lord Darlington?
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: No, not the world. Who are the people the world takes seriously? All the dull people one can think of, from the Bishops down to the bores. I should like you to take me very seriously, Lady Windermere, you more than any one else in life.
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: Why—why me?
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: After a slight hesitation .
Because I think we might be great friends. Let us be great friends. You may want a friend some day.
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: Why do you say that?
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Oh!—we all want friends at times.
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: I think we’re very good friends already, Lord Darlington. We can always remain so as long as you don’t—
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Don’t what?
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: Don’t spoil it by saying extravagant silly things to me. You think I am a Puritan, I suppose? Well, I have something of the Puritan in me. I was brought up like that. I am glad of it. My mother died when I was a mere child. I lived always with Lady Julia, my father’s elder sister, you know. She was stern to me, but she taught me what the world is forgetting, the difference that there is between what is right and what is wrong. She allowed of no compromise. I allow of none.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: My dear Lady Windermere!
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: Leaning back on the sofa .
You look on me as being behind the age.—Well, I am! I should be sorry to be on the same level as an age like this.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: You think the age very bad?
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: Yes. Nowadays people seem to look on life as a speculation. It is not a speculation. It is a sacrament. Its ideal is Love. Its purification is sacrifice.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Smiling .
Oh, anything is better than being sacrificed!
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: Leaning forward .
Don’t say that.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: I do say it. I feel it—I know it.
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: Enter PARKER C.
The men want to know if they are to put the carpets on the terrace for to-night, my lady?
units.name: PARKER

units.text: You don’t think it will rain, Lord Darlington, do you?
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: I won’t hear of its raining on your birthday!
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: Tell them to do it at once, Parker.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Exit PARKER C.
Still seated .

Do you think then—of course I am only putting an imaginary instance—do you think that in the case of a young married couple, say about two years married, if the husband suddenly becomes the intimate friend of a woman of—well, more than doubtful character—is always calling upon her, lunching with her, and probably paying her bills—do you think that the wife should not console herself?
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: Frowning .
Console herself?
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Yes, I think she should—I think she has the right.
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: Because the husband is vile—should the wife be vile also?
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Vileness is a terrible word, Lady Windermere.
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON

units.text: It is a terrible thing, Lord Darlington.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Do you know I am afraid that good people do a great deal of harm in this world. Certainly the greatest harm they do is that they make badness of such extraordinary importance. It is absurd to divide people into good and bad. People are either charming or tedious. I take the side of the charming, and you, Lady Windermere, can’t help belonging to them.
units.name: LORD DARLINGTON
